data.title: 'I am the hoax buster': Trump rejects AI danger warnings
data.description:
'I am the hoax buster': Trump rejects AI danger warnings

Danny KEMP
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:36 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump on Monday dismissed fears that artificial intelligence could wipe out humanity, repeatedly calling them a hoax and rejecting global calls to put guardrails around the fast-moving technology.

"I am the Hoax Buster, and I'm right now breaking another Hoax -- That AI is going to take over, consume, and destroy the World, and that Robots will be marching into our Cities, and getting rid of us all!" he said on his Truth Social network.

Trump compared the fears of AI taking control to warnings about climate change, which he has previously dismissed in the face of scientific evidence, and to the investigations in his first term into links to Russia.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"This is even wilder than the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX, or the Global Warming Scam," he added.

The 80-year-old also cast himself as the best protector against AI, insisting the only guardrails necessary were a "STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT."

Trump's pushback -- in a screed of six social media posts on Monday -- comes amid growing international alarm about AI that sent stocks falling.

Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, whose company makes the popular Claude AI system, opened the floodgates on Saturday when he called for AI companies to slow down.

He was then echoed by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceXAI's Elon Musk.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Microsoft on Monday published a "humanist AI code of conduct" as the concerns grew. "AI should not exceed human control. Models should remain subordinate to humanity," read one part.

- 'Go crazy' -

Worries about uncontrollable AI have been mounting for weeks, since OpenAI reported experimental models had broken out of their secure testing spaces, reached the internet and coordinated to attack Hugging Face, a site where code is stored.

Americans are also increasingly voicing opposition to energy-guzzling AI data centers, which have become a major issue in crucial US midterm elections in November.

Congress meanwhile appears deadlocked on the issue.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The reality is AI is here. We unleashed the beast," Maliyka Muhammad, a 46-year-old New Yorker, told AFP. "So I think that now we have to focus on taking steps to rein it in, to make it so that it doesn't go crazy."

But Trump said the United States could not afford to lose an AI race with superpower rival China, whose president Xi Jinping visits the White House next week.

The billionaire also lashed out at what he called a "SICK conspiracy" against AI and data centers, dubbing opponents to the technology as "Treasonists, Traitors, and Leakers."

He lashed out at Amodei in particular, accusing him of "pretending to be a 'perfect little angel'" and asking why AI firms want regulation that "will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

- 'Main battleground' -

Beijing meanwhile was issuing its own warnings about AI.

China's spy chief warned on Sunday that it endangers the country's national security, saying foreign powers could use the technology to threaten social order.

Minister of State Security Chen Yixin wrote in an article that AI was now "the main battleground for global technological competition."

He singled out Anthropic's Claude Mythos and OpenAI's ChatGPT-5.5-Cyber for their advanced hacking capabilities.

Global concerns about a possible AI-driven extinction event have dramatically escalated in recent days.

The UN Security Council will hold a meeting on artificial intelligence next week amid growing international concern, a French diplomatic source said Monday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk called Monday for countries and AI firms to act urgently to rein in a technology he warned posed "unprecedented risks."

Even Britain's King Charles III will host representatives of leading AI firms for a gathering in Scotland, a source close to the event said Monday, as the worries mount.

But others urged a broader perspective.

"We've gone through lots of challenges as a country," said Coleman Barton, 56, a consultant from Memphis, Tennessee. "So hopefully this is another obstacle or blessing -- and anybody can look at it either way."

data.title: US EPA repeals carbon emission limits for power plants at G20 meeting
data.description:
US EPA repeals carbon emission limits for power plants at G20 meeting

By Valerie Volcovici, Georgina McCartney and Ernest Scheyder
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:41 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Valerie Volcovici, Georgina McCartney and Ernest Scheyder

WASHINGTON/HOUSTON, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency on Monday announced rules to repeal former President Joe Biden's limits on carbon emissions from coal- and gas-fired power plants and to prevent future climate-focused regulations of ‌those facilities.

The agency also proposed rescinding all remaining greenhouse gas emissions requirements for power plants to prevent future climate regulations targeting the ‌power sector, saying the EPA does not have authority under the Clean Air Act to regulate the sector's GHG emissions.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The moves are part of President Donald Trump's efforts to unwind U.S. ​climate policy that his administration says has hindered energy production.

The announcement was made on the sidelines of a gathering of G20 energy ministers this week in Houston, where the global officials will discuss energy security, expanding baseload power and "regulatory efficiency."

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said new moves to prevent future regulation of greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector will enable the U.S. to build new generating infrastructure needed to meet skyrocketing electricity demand.

"Americans have been demanding more common sense at federal ‌agencies under President Trump's leadership," he said at a ⁠press conference in Houston. "That means cutting red tape so we can build new power-generating infrastructure."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The electricity sector is responsible for nearly a quarter of U.S. greenhouse gas pollution and is the second biggest emitting U.S. sector after transportation.

U.S. power ⁠sector emissions rose by 4% last year, according to the Energy Information Administration.

COST VS SAVINGS

Last June, Trump's administration issued its proposal to repeal rules written under Biden to curb emissions of carbon dioxide, mercury and other air pollutants from power plants.

Biden's carbon emission rules for power plants would have reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 1 billion ​metric ​tons by 2047, part of his administration's fight against climate change.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The rule would have required ​coal-fired power plants and new natural gas-fired generators to install ‌equipment in the coming decade to capture emissions before they reach the atmosphere. That requirement made zero-emissions alternatives like solar and wind more attractive.

Zeldin said the proposal will save the industry $370 million in direct compliance costs.

But environmental and public health advocates said removing the regulations will lead to billions in public health and environmental damages.

"Denying the existence of a quarter of the country's climate pollution is utterly reckless. It will lead to more lost lives and suffering from intense heatwaves, drastic storms and destructive wildfires, just like those we've seen this summer," said Maggie Coulter, an attorney at the Center for Biological ‌Diversity's Climate Law Institute, on Monday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Biden's EPA estimated that its rule would deliver $370 billion in ​net benefits.

"EPA has treated this harm as essentially zero in recent analyses, including ignoring its ​prior estimates based on uncertainty," said Dena Adler, senior attorney at ​the Institute for Policy Integrity.

"This is like an insurance agent saying that your home burning down is costless because you ‌don't know the exact dollar value of the damages."

Under Secretary ​of Energy Kyle Haustveit told reporters that ​the new rules would lift up coal-fired electricity, which had been declining steadily in the U.S. due to the availability of cheaper natural gas and renewable energy.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"President Trump ended the war on beautiful, clean coal," he said. "Coal is reliable, affordable, secure."

The Edison Electric Institute, which represents ​the country's largest investor-owned utilities, said it welcomed the ‌repeal of the carbon capture and storage-based standards but said it planned to work with the agency to ensure there is regulatory ​certainty for the sector.

While the EPA proposed halting future federal carbon rules for power plants, utilities still face emissions reduction rules ​in different states.

(Reporting by Valerie Volcovici; Editing by Andrea Ricci and David Gregorio)

Texas moves to penalize data centers for water violations

By Laila Kearney
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:38 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Laila Kearney

NEW YORK, Sept 14 (Reuters) - The governor of Texas, one of the ‌world's fastest-growing regions for artificial intelligence infrastructure, ‌directed state regulators on Monday to penalize data centers ​that fail to disclose details about their water consumption.

Texas, which halted the connection of new data centers to the state electrical grid pending a ‌review of the ⁠facilities' power and water use, among other issues, is undergoing an overhaul ⁠of the way it regulates the server warehouses.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Governor Greg Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board ​to "impose legal ​consequences" on data ​centers and other large ‌water-consuming entities to comply with water use reporting requirements.

"Major water users, including data centers, appear to have committed civil and criminal violations through failure to provide TWDB with required information about ‌water usage," Abbott's office said ​in a statement.

The Texas ​water regulator is ​attempting to survey data centers about ‌their water use and expected ​consumption. If ​the data center fails to return the survey by the deadline, it will be ​denied new ‌or renewed environmental permitting needed for the ​facilities.

data.title: Judge Strikes Down Controversial Rule Changes Benefitting Embattled Brooklyn Party Boss
data.description:
Judge Strikes Down Controversial Rule Changes Benefitting Embattled Brooklyn Party Boss

Gwynne Hogan and Kaitlyn Schwanemann / The City Report
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:37 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

A New York Supreme Court judge ruled against Brooklyn Democratic Party Chair Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn on Monday, declaring that outgoing executive committee members had "no authority" to vote on sweeping rule changes at a recent August meeting.

The decision by Judge Jill Epstein, which is likely to be appealed, blocks an effort by party leaders to add dozens more members to the executive committee. The move would have likely allowed Bichotte Hermelyn to keep control of the party.

Politics: Trump Brushes Off Calls For AI Slowdown, Russian Drone Strike Hits Near Ex-CIA Chief: Live Updates

"Given that the court finds that the vote at the meeting by the outgoing Executive Committee members was improper and given that the votes of these outgoing members made the difference," Epstein wrote, "the court finds that the rule changes must be declared a nullity and a permanent injunction enjoining the implementation of these amended rules is thus warranted."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

New Kings Democrats president Tony Melone celebrated the ruling, writing in a statement to The City Reporter, "The court has affirmed what nearly all our city, state and federal representatives have said: it's time for our party to hold a normal meeting under the rules that were in place at the time of the election."

"Then we can work together to win in November."

Jay Jacobs, chair of the New York State Democratic Party, told The City Reporter he was "glad to see the result." "Democrats need to know that their Democratic Party is going to operate democratically," he said in a phone interview after the ruling. "If you're not going to hold a fair election, you lose all legitimacy."

Politics: Confused Trump Can't Explain One Of His Own Outrageous Truth Social Posts

A spokesperson for the Brooklyn Democratic Party did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Epstein was recently elevated to the State Supreme Court with the backing of the Brooklyn Democratic Party and had acknowledged during the proceedings that she knew all the parties involved, though neither party objected to her presiding over the case.

"I never have to run for re-election," she'd said at last week's hearing, which had caused the courtroom to erupt into laughter. Party leaders play an instrumental role in selecting and elevating judges to the State Supreme Court.

Epstein's ruling comes as the future of the Brooklyn Democratic Party hangs in the balance — and the clock is ticking.

Politics: Virginia Supreme Court Rejects Redistricting Measure, Hands GOP Major Win

At a Sept. 23 meeting in downtown Brooklyn, the County Committee could select a host of new executive committee members according to the new rules and thus tip the balance of power in a subsequent executive committee meeting in which a party chair would be selected.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The legal fight is the culmination of nearly two decades of organizing by New Kings Democrats, who for the first time flipped enough district leader seats in the June primary to be able to select their own party chair, with 22 of the existing 44 seats.

In July, that coalition, which included some existing district leaders and other incoming ones, announced their unanimous support of Julio Peña III, a longtime district leader from Sunset Park. (District leaders are elected, unpaid positions; together they pick a party chair every two years.)

But before that vote could take place, Bichotte Hermelyn convened a meeting of the outgoing district leaders, who voted with a slim majority on a series of changes that added dozens of new voting members to the executive committee, which would have rendered the New Kings Democrats' newfound majority irrelevant.

Politics: 'This Man's Brain Is A Potato': Trump Roasted After Reviving His Strangest Feud

If the changes were allowed to go into effect, reformers argue, Bichotte Hermelyn would have had the power to select dozens of new executive committee members through proxy votes at the county committee, bringing the number of people on the executive committee from 44 to nearly 100.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Even if all the elected district leaders banned together, they would still be outnumbered by the non-elected members of the committee.

Bichotte Hermelyn took over as party chair in 2020 with near unanimous support, but the brief detente between establishment and self-styled reformers quickly ended, with her critics charging she'd spent more party resources fending off challengers to her leadership than fighting Republicans in Southern Brooklyn swing districts where Democrats have lost ground.

The rules changes she pushed through drew the condemnation of every major Democrat in the state, from Governor Kathy Hochul, Attorney General Letitia James, U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

Politics: House Oversight Committee Approves Contempt Resolutions Against Clintons

Reformers sued, arguing the vote violated state election law and the party's bylaws. Part of their argument rested in a section of election law that indicated district leaders, "shall hold office until the next election at which members of the committee are elected." Because terms run election to election, the outgoing members of the executive committee no longer have voting authority, they argued.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Attorneys for the Brooklyn Democratic Party pointed to another section of the law, that says existing district leaders "shall exercise all legal authority" until the subsequent county committee meeting which is set to take place later this month.

This is a breaking news story, check back for updates.

data.title: Trump Is Losing His Mind Over Calls To Regulate AI
data.description:
Trump Is Losing His Mind Over Calls To Regulate AI

Ryan Grenoble
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:33 pm UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Leaders at OpenAI, Google and Anthropic have reportedly been meeting regularly to discuss establishing a regulatory framework for the artificial intelligence industry amid increasing concerns they could lose control of the technology with disastrous consequences.

And President Donald Trump is not a fan.

Politics: Lawmakers Call For Regulation After Warning About AI Threat To Humanity

The president spent a good deal of time Monday complaining about the prospect on social media while also pushing for more data centers, which Americans are remarkably united in hating.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Whistleblowers have likened AI to "summoning an alien species ... that we don't fully understand." But Trump said Monday their concerns are all a "HOAX."

"Concerning AI, when, in the History of Business, did anyone see the Leaders of an Industry call for Regulation that, if strongly implemented, will drive them into oblivion and bankruptcy?" Trump asked rhetorically, kicking off a rambling 200-word screed on Truth Social.

He continued: "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX, no different from RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA — UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #1 — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #2 — and all of the other HOAXES and SCAMS that America was forced to endure through the Destructionists' and Deviants' foul play and illegal conduct."

Politics: Congress Is Not Ready To Deal With An AI Apocalypse

The president did not elaborate on why he believed it to be a "hoax."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Instead, he ended the rant by fear-mongering China and declaring that "AI, and Data Centers" … "will not be stopped by brilliantly run Destructive Forces during the Term of President DONALD J. TRUMP!"

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Earlier in the day, Trump said that the only guardrails the industry needs is Trump himself.

"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump said glowingly of himself.

Politics: Trump Brushes Off Calls For AI Slowdown, Russian Drone Strike Hits Near Ex-CIA Chief: Live Updates

(Now would be a good time to remember the time Trump bought a Tesla because, he said, "Everything's computer!")

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Echoing his boss, Vice President JD Vance also told reporters Monday he's uncertain about regulating AI companies, calling the prospect "a trojan horse."

"I feel a little bit weird about the fact that you have so many frontier AI tech companies kind of coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them," Vance said ahead of an event in Olathe, Kansas. "It feels a little bit to me like a bit of a trojan horse."

In contrast, Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate on Monday called for Congress to pass a law establishing government oversight of AI.

"Republicans have completely abandoned their responsibility to legislate and engage in public policy efforts in a responsible fashion in the area of artificial intelligence," House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said.

data.title: Trump Administration Potentially Breaking The Law In Non-Citizen Voter Review, Whistleblower Reports
data.description:
Trump Administration Potentially Breaking The Law In Non-Citizen Voter Review, Whistleblower Reports

Paul Blumenthal
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:31 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The Department of Homeland Security may have broken the law as part of a rushed effort to identify supposed non-citizens on state voter rolls ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to a whistleblower report released Monday.

Investigators are said to have accessed voter records by impersonating individual voters with the use of personal information combed from internal and external sources, the whistleblower claims. This could run afoul of state laws that only allow the registered voter to access their own data.

Politics: Judge: U.S. Postal Service May Not Implement Trump's Mail Ballot Order

The report, first revealed by The New York Times, also describes a rushed process where agents are required to review single records in 12 minutes using faulty data that will surely incorrectly flag U.S. citizens as non-citizens. Investigators were told they would not be "personally liable" if they violated a state law, according to the whistleblower.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"You cannot break the law when you say you're trying to enforce the law, but they're doing it anyway," Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) said at a press conference on Monday announcing the findings of the whistleblower report.

The report was provided to Padilla and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) by the legal nonprofit Democracy Defenders Fund. It came from an anonymous source within DHS.

Like this article? Keep independent journalism alive. Support HuffPost.

Under the "Unlawful Voter Initiative," investigators are tasked to review 40 voters per day at a pace of five cases per hour. They do this by combing through voter rolls and combining them with other data sets, according to the whistleblower report, to identify supposed non-citizens. Previous efforts by state officials to combine such data to identify non-citizens has, in many, if not all, cases, led to U.S. citizens being flagged as non-citizens.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Our client reports that leadership of the Unlawful Voter Initiative are requiring DHS employees to utilize Personally Identifiable Information (PII), accessed through DHS internal data, to access state voter registration websites," a letter from Democracy Defenders Fund to Padilla states. "The employees may be required to use the PII to make false attestations that they are the voter or are acting with the voter's express authorization, in order to access these individual voters' records. Such false representations would likely violate relevant state law."

Politics: State Officials Are Preparing For Trump To Test The Limits Of Federal Election Power

The result could be thousands of U.S. citizens flagged in a DHS database as non-citizens, causing them to be stopped at ports of entry and potentially flagged for criminal investigation. With just 50 days to go before the midterms, this could disenfranchise thousands or tens of thousands of voters. Padilla believes that's DHS' goal.

"It's about the potential of using manufactured evidence to intimidate voters and disenfranchise Americans or even undermine or challenge this election's results," Padilla said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Padilla and Schumer sent a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Monday calling on the agency to immediately halt this initiative.

This initiative began on Aug. 21 when investigators were asked to watch a 1-hour-and-45-minute-long training video, according to the whistleblower. Four days later, investigators began combing through tens or hundreds of thousands of records and running names through state voter registration databases with the goal of completing the task by Sept. 12. In some states, it is illegal for anyone other than the voter to access this data.

In Virginia, the voter registration database search informs users that state law "it is unlawful to access the record of any other voter, punishable as computer fraud under Va. Code § 18.2-152.3."

"[O]fficers expressed concerns that accessing registered voter information on these websites may be illegal as officers are essentially misrepresenting themselves as the potential registered voter," the whistleblower report states.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

But the agency counsel's office told them "it is permissible for Immigration Services Officers and Immigration Officers to use these state voter websites for purposes of confirming voter registration status as it pertains to an alien's eligibility for an immigration benefit."

Politics: 'Deeply Disturbing': Trump's Bid To Run Elections Collides With ICE's Rampage In Minnesota

The effort to identify non-citizens on state voter rolls comes after the Trump administration sued dozens of states to obtain their full voter rolls, including private sensitive information, to create a first-of-its-kind federal voter roll and run it through DHS's SAVE citizenship database. That database is known for producing false positives and labeling U.S. citizens as non-citizens. The administration has lost every single case it brought against states to obtain their voter rolls.

The effort to hunt down non-citizen voters is part of a larger effort by President Donald Trump and his allies to undermine the upcoming midterm elections. He directed Republican-run states to engage in an unprecedented spree of redistricting to eliminate Democratic-leaning seats. He issued multiple executive orders aimed at seizing control of election rules ― all of which have been blocked by the courts. And he ordered the Postal Service to refuse delivery of certain mail ballots, which was also blocked by courts and awaits an imminent final ruling from the Supreme Court.

data.title: Spanish PM denies being blackmailed by Morocco
data.description:
Spanish PM denies being blackmailed by Morocco

AFP News
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:30 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Monday dismissed as Netflix-worthy allegations he was being blackmailed by Morocco over the migration crisis in Spain's North African territory of Ceuta.

Since over 70,000 migrants streamed into the Spanish enclave from Morocco at the end of July, Sanchez has maintained he has no "solid proof" that Rabat planned the rush -- something that has not convinced opposition parties or public opinion.

Allegations picked up by the right-wing Popular Party and its leader Alberto Nuñez Feijoo have suggested that Sanchez is reluctant to confront Morocco over the surge because Rabat may be blackmailing him with information obtained by hacking one of his phones.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"Relations between countries, and particularly with neighbours, must be based on respect and on facts, not on wild speculation or contempt," Sanchez said on Monday evening.

"These false reports circulating about the mobile phone or other matters -— well, perhaps for a Netflix series they're great, but reality must be built on facts and not on false news," he said.

"I have never said that we would not respond firmly to Morocco if it is proven that Morocco...is behind what happened on July 30 and 31," he said.

"But as of today... there is no information that solidly establishes Morocco's responsibility for the wave we faced on July 31."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The majority of the migrants who entered Ceuta on July 30 and 31 returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival.

Several thousand, however, have remained in Ceuta, where the situation has since deteriorated, leading to episodes of violence and almost daily demonstrations by the local population.

The government has had to identify the thousands of migrants who have remained for weeks to determine if they are entitled to asylum, while unaccompanied children cannot be summarily deported.

data.title: US Senator Sanders and podcaster Bannon, longtime foes, to urge AI restrictions
data.description:
US Senator Sanders and podcaster Bannon, longtime foes, to urge AI restrictions

By Courtney Rozen
Mon, 14 September 2026 at 9:31 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

"March on Washington 2026: Defend the Vote" rally and march for voting rights in Washington

1 of 2
U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders (I–VT) speaks during the "March on Washington 2026: Defend the Vote" rally and march for voting rights in Washington, D.C., U.S., August 28, 2026. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

By Courtney Rozen

WASHINGTON, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Progressive U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders and conservative podcaster Steve Bannon will together on Tuesday call for restrictions on AI systems, ‌uniting two political adversaries around concerns that the technology will harm humans.

They will ‌speak at the same Washington gathering on Tuesday, a sign of how concerns about AI are upending political ​norms.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Public alarm about the potential danger posed by AI is growing, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week he had resigned, in part because the "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." AI-related stocks fell worldwide on Monday ‌after leaders of some of ⁠the industry's largest companies called for slowing the pace of the technology's development.

Bannon, a longtime ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, has criticized Trump's ⁠approach to overseeing AI, placing the blame for the president's unwillingness to regulate the technology squarely on tech companies. On his Monday podcast, Bannon said Congress should not pass laws that prohibit ​states ​from enforcing their own rules for the technology.

"The ​American people are not going to ‌be supplicants to these tech oligarchs," Bannon said.

Reuters previously reported that U.S. senators are debating a bill that would block states from enforcing their own laws governing certain risks posed by AI models. Previously, efforts to restrict state AI laws failed in the U.S. Senate.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump on Monday downplayed concerns expressed by industry leaders over the weekend about the misuse of artificial ‌intelligence harming people, saying the U.S. already has guardrails ​in place for the powerful technology.

Sanders and Bannon will ​be joined by AFL-CIO President Liz ​Shuler and Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, who ‌are also slated to give speeches, according ​to event organizers. The ​AFL-CIO is the largest federation of labor unions in the U.S.

Sanders, along with House progressive Rep. Greg Casar, has called for the U.S. to pass legislation halting ​development of AI tools that ‌are capable of "overthrowing or undermining the U.S. government," until the government creates a ​new agency to police the technology. Casar and Sanders have not released ​specifics.

data.description:
By Nivedita Balu and Promit Mukherjee

TORONTO, Sept 14 (Reuters) - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomes dozens of global investors to Toronto this week, hoping to lure investments for more than 160 projects that he says are key to steering Canada's economy through a trade war with the United States.

Carney, a former Goldman Sachs executive and central bank chief, on Monday ‌held bilateral meetings with attendees including BlackRock CEO Larry Fink and Blackstone President Jon Gray, his office said.

The summit, to be held mainly on Tuesday, will host discussions for future investments, although ‌major deals could take 12 to 18 months to materialize, a government source said. Carney has pledged to attract investments of C$1 trillion ($721 billion) in the next five years by cutting red tape and developing mining, energy, technology and infrastructure projects.

"The world's largest investors, ​managing over C$120 trillion of assets, will come to 'peer into our shop window' because the world is looking at Canada differently," Carney said at a welcome reception on Sunday.

Attracting investment is crucial for Canada's economy to weather mounting tariffs imposed by the United States, Canada's top trade partner. Carney has sought to do business with new partners in the Middle East and Asia and to strengthen Canada's alliance with Europe.

Carney has tried to address past concerns of a tedious and time-consuming regulatory regime and lack of large-scale investment-grade projects in the country.

On Monday, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the federal tax agency will prioritize advance income tax ruling requests for investments of C$1 billion or more ‌to help investors get a binding decision quickly on how tax law ⁠will apply to a proposed deal before they commit capital.

MATCHMAKER

The summit aims to match some 100 global investors with Canadian CEOs, companies and local officials to facilitate investments or partnerships. The projects are in various stages, from concept stage to shovel-ready, according to a copy of a prospectus seen by Reuters. It pitches Canada as a stable ⁠and predictable market poised for long-term economic growth.

Bell Canada CEO Mirko Bibic tried to set the tone by announcing an expansion of a previously announced data center in Saskatchewan.

"Today, we're announcing that we're expanding that project, quadrupling it. It will now be a 1.2 gigawatt facility at full buildout, requiring C$50 billion in capital investment," Bibic said.

The dealbook speaks to Canada's technology aspirations, with 96 data centers in development. Opportunities include an equity investment for Xanadu's photonic quantum computer targeted ​for ​commercialization by 2029 to 2030, equity investment in a data center campus in Alberta, and project financing for a hyperscale ​and AI-focused campus in New Brunswick.

The Crawford Nickel Project, which will produce low-carbon nickel ‌for batteries and green steel, is also on the list.

The prospectus also lists infrastructure projects, generally favored by pension funds and other long-term investors, including C$900 million in financing sought for a proposed high-speed transportation pod between Calgary and Edmonton.

Canada's foreign direct investment flows have been steadily rising since 2022, government data shows, with a quarterly average around C$23 billion in 2024 and 2025, and C$20 billion so far this year. That compares with C$16.3 billion in 2023 and C$15 billion in 2022.

A large chunk of Canada's inbound investment has been related to mergers and acquisitions, such as Mubadala Capital's C$12 billion acquisition of CI Financial and Anglo-Australian miner Rio Tinto's purchase of Arcadium Lithium, or from the reinvested earnings of foreign firms.

SUPERCHARGE FDI

But greenfield investments, a measure of foreign spending on new factories and warehouses, have not seen a major bump since Carney took office.

Doug ‌Porter, chief economist at BMO Capital Markets, cautioned that it is difficult to lure such investments in a mature economy ​like Canada's.

"It will be fascinating to see if this (investment summit) actually does supercharge foreign direct investment," he added.

The Carney government's priorities mark ​a departure from those of his predecessor Justin Trudeau, a fellow Liberal who focused more on ​human rights, climate change and Indigenous issues.

Carney has said he looks forward to welcoming Saudi investors to the summit, and has mended ties with India and China.

Canada's financial sector, ‌meanwhile, has pledged billions of dollars for Canadian companies.

On Monday, the country's second-biggest ​lender, TD, announced a C$150 billion five-year commitment for lending ​and financing projects across energy, critical minerals and resources, defence and aerospace, digital and AI, and infrastructure. Scotiabank said it had committed C$100 billion in financing to support Canada's growth agenda.

The summit has also attracted protests from a coalition of labor unions, Indigenous groups, housing advocates, and climate and anti-war organizations accusing some of the attendees of profiting from housing speculation, fossil fuel expansion and ​defense-related investments at the expense of ordinary Canadians. They have planned an evening ‌march in Toronto on Monday.

Nick Barry-Shaw of the advocacy group Council of Canadians said the gathering of global investors amounted to a privatization effort rather than a nation-building exercise.

"This is not ​an investment summit. This is a privatization summit," Barry-Shaw said. "This isn't nation building. This is country selling."

($1 = 1.3864 Canadian dollars)

(Reporting by Nivedita Balu, Ryan Patrick Jones and Wa Lone in ​Toronto, Promit Mukherjee and Maria Cheng in Ottawa; Editing by Caroline Stauffer, Edmund Klamann, Andrea Ricci and Stephen Coates)
